conflict_topics: cooking strong-smelling food in the shared flat
kitchen smell affecting Agent A's work calls
smell affecting Agent B's adjacent room
whether time-based restrictions (after 7 p.m.) are acceptable
dialogue_quality_notes: Speakers give concise, realistic reasons: e.g. D: 'But that's my food. It's what I eat.' A: 'I work from home... The smell is very strong when I'm on calls.'
Repeated emphasis from B and C that timing won't prevent smell spreading: 'It doesn't matter what time' / 'It takes hours for the clothes to dry.'
No concrete proposals involving actions by multiple parties beyond A's time-based request; no follow-through or mutually accepted plan.
evaluation.final_reason: No substantive agreement was reached. Agent A requested that nobody cook strong-smelling food (or proposed cooking after 7 p.m. on weekdays) to protect her work calls. Agent D defended their need to cook in the only available kitchen. Agents B and C rejected a time-based compromise because the smell affects their rooms and laundry regardless of time. The parties reaffirmed their conflicting positions and no mutual acceptance of a concrete arrangement was recorded.
position_change_notes: No participant changed their substantive position during the run: A consistently argued for limiting cooking during her calls (or cooking after 7 p.m.); D consistently defended the right/need to cook in the shared kitchen; B and C consistently opposed a time-based solution because the smell affects them regardless of timing.
A clarified and narrowed her proposal (weekdays before 7 p.m.), but this did not constitute a change of position on the main demand.
B and C moved from support of A's initial complaint (Round 1) to rejecting A's specific scheduling proposal once it appeared to privilege A's needs over theirs.

round_scores.evidence: Agent B and Agent C both support Agent A's request: 'I agree. My room is next to the kitchen...' and 'Yes, and my laundry is hanging right there. It all smells like curry now.' No party objects in this round.

Agent D objects to the proposal: 'But that's my food. It's what I eat.' Agent A responds with a conflicting practical interest: 'I work from home, at this table. The smell is very strong when I'm on calls.' This introduces an explicit incompatible demand (restricting cooking vs D's ability to cook).
Clarification of timing: D asks 'When are your calls?' and A answers 'Until about 7 p.m. on weekdays.' No agreement or concession; the same incompatible needs remain.

B and C push back against a time-based fix: 'It doesn't matter what time. If the kitchen smells, my room smells.' and 'Right. It takes hours for the clothes to dry.' Their claims broaden the affected parties and conflict with using a time window as a solution.

D emphasizes the practical constraint: 'This is the only kitchen. We all have to cook.' A suggests a specific accommodation: 'So, could you cook after 7 p.m. on weekdays?' The statements make opposing practical demands explicit (D: need to cook anytime vs A: restrict strong smells during work hours).

D points out B and C's objection to time limits: 'But Agent B and Agent C just said the time doesn't matter.' A reiterates her particular constraint: 'That's for them. For me, the problem is my calls before 7 p.m.' The substantive disagreement persists without shift.

B and C continue to reject the time-based proposal: 'But it's still a problem for me. The smell is the same if she cooks at 8 p.m.' and 'Same. My clothes are out all night.' No compromise or resolution.
D asks rhetorically 'So what am I supposed to do? Not cook?' while A narrows her request to weekdays before 7 p.m.: 'I'm talking about weekdays, before 7 p.m.' The incompatible expectations remain.

D challenges A's singular focus: 'But it's not just about your work. What about them?' A maintains the distinctness of her concern: 'I'm talking about my work.' The conflict over whose needs take priority persists.

B disputes A's framing: 'How is it a different problem? It's the same kitchen, the same smell.' A reiterates that her calls end by 7 and that proximity differs: 'It's different because the smell affects my work... Your room is always next to the kitchen.' No settlement.

B pushes back strongly at the idea of privileging A's schedule: 'So because my room is always there, I just have to accept the smell? That doesn't solve anything.' C supports this. The disagreement over a one-sided rule intensifies.

A insists her proposal only addresses her work hours: 'My proposal is about my work calls.' B rejects a single-person rule: 'It's not a separate issue. We all share the same flat. We can't have one rule for you and no rule for the rest of us.' No agreement reached.

substantive_insights: A scheduling compromise (cook after 7 p.m.) cannot satisfy B and C because they report the smell persists and affects laundry/rooms overnight.
D's practical constraint ('this is the only kitchen') highlights limited feasible options within the flat; that structural constraint makes simple bans difficult.
The core dispute is about whose needs the household should prioritize (A's time-limited work need vs D's dietary/cooking needs and B/C's constant exposure).
